title: One Borrower, Four Answers: Asking About Residency Status at an AI Mortgage Point of Sale After FHA Dropped Non-Permanent Residents
summary: Since May 2025, a non-permanent resident cannot get an FHA loan, can still get a Fannie Mae loan on the same terms as a citizen, and gets different answers again from Freddie Mac and USDA depending on their documents. Regulation B lets a lender ask about immigration status, and the 2023 CFPB and DOJ statement on noncitizen borrowers was withdrawn in January 2026. How we designed the residency question in an AI point of sale so it routes a borrower to a program they qualify for instead of screening them out.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of retail and consumer-direct lending, point-of-sale and digital product owners, and fair lending officers at lenders who originate FHA alongside conventional loans. Also anyone whose loan officers or intake scripts still treat "are you a U.S. citizen?" as a yes-or-no gate.


## The Rule Changed for One Program and Not the Others


On March 26, 2025, HUD issued[Mortgagee Letter 2025-09](https://www.hud.gov/sites/default/files/OCHCO/documents/2025-09hsgml.pdf) , which removed the non-permanent resident sections from the FHA Single Family Housing Policy Handbook. For case numbers assigned on or after May 25, 2025, a borrower must be a U.S. citizen or a lawful permanent resident to get an FHA-insured loan. Citizens of the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau remain eligible under the compacts of free association.


Fannie Mae did not follow.[Selling Guide B2-2-02](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-2-02/non-us-citizen-borrower-eligibility-requirements) still says Fannie Mae purchases loans made to non-U.S. citizens who are lawful permanent or non-permanent residents under the same terms available to U.S. citizens. The lender decides what documentation establishes legal presence, and by delivering the loan it represents and warrants that the borrower is legally present. Freddie Mac's Guide, at section 5103.2, also accepts lawfully residing non-permanent residents, but does not treat DACA recipients as eligible, which Fannie Mae has said it does when the borrower's lawful presence is documented. USDA's guaranteed program ended its temporary non-citizen waiver in March 2025, and under[7 CFR 3555.151](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/subtitle-B/chapter-XXXV/part-3555/subpart-D/section-3555.151) an applicant has to show they are a citizen, a non-citizen national or a "qualified alien," a term that is broader than permanent residency.


So the same borrower, say a software engineer on an H-1B visa with a 760 score and 12% down, is ineligible for FHA, eligible for a Fannie Mae conventional loan, eligible for Freddie Mac, and probably ineligible for USDA. A DACA recipient with the same profile gets a different set of answers again. Before May 2025, the answer for most non-permanent residents was "yes" almost everywhere, so a lot of intake logic never had to tell these cases apart.


## What Regulation B Allows You to Ask


The fair lending question comes first, because a residency question that is asked badly looks like national origin discrimination.[Regulation B at 12 CFR 1002.6(b)(7)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/6/) says a creditor may consider an applicant's immigration status or status as a permanent resident, and may consider any additional information that may be necessary to ascertain the creditor's rights and remedies regarding repayment. The official commentary explains that a creditor may tell apart a long-time permanent resident from someone in the country on a temporary visa, and that refusing credit because someone is not a citizen is not, on its own, national origin discrimination.


In October 2023, the CFPB and the Department of Justice issued a joint statement on fair lending and noncitizen borrowers, which warned that overbroad reliance on immigration status could violate ECOA. On January 12, 2026, both agencies[withdrew it](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-12/html/2026-00328.htm) , saying the statement may have given a false impression that ECOA limits how lenders weigh immigration or citizenship status. The withdrawal changes federal guidance. It does not change ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, or state laws, and several states examine for disparate impact under their own statutes regardless of what federal agencies say.


The practical line has not moved much. Asking about residency status is allowed. Treating a non-citizen worse than the loan program requires, or using a residency question as a proxy for where someone is from, is where the risk sits.


## Where Point-of-Sale Logic Goes Wrong


We see three failure patterns when we review intake flows lenders already run.


The first is a binary citizenship gate. The application asks "Are you a U.S. citizen?" and a "no" either ends the flow or routes the borrower to a slower, manual queue. After ML 2025-09, some flows added a hard stop on "no" for any FHA-shaped borrower, which is right for FHA and wrong for every conventional option the same borrower might qualify for.


The second is asking for the wrong document at the wrong time. A Social Security card does not establish immigration status, and an EAD card, a visa and a green card prove different things. Asking every non-citizen for every document is slower and treats them differently from citizens in a way the program does not require. Asking for none of them until underwriting means the loan can fail for a reason that was knowable in the first conversation.


The third is the loan officer's own answer. A loan officer who learned "non-citizens can't get FHA anymore" may tell a green-card holder they are ineligible, or tell a non-permanent resident they cannot buy at all. Both are wrong, and both are the kind of statement that turns into a complaint or a fair lending exam finding.


## How We Designed the Residency Question


When we rebuilt the residency step in our[POS](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/pos) , the design rule was that the question exists to choose a program, not to decide whether to serve the borrower. That decision shaped four things.


The question is the URLA question, asked once. The Uniform Residential Loan Application already asks whether the borrower is a U.S. citizen, a permanent resident alien or a non-permanent resident alien. The POS asks it in that form, the same way for every applicant, and does not ask about country of birth or nationality, which no program we support needs at intake.


The answer narrows programs instead of ending the conversation. A "non-permanent resident alien" answer removes FHA from the options the borrower sees and keeps conventional and any portfolio products the lender offers. The borrower is told plainly why FHA is not available, with the program rule, because "you don't qualify" without a reason is the kind of statement that becomes a complaint. Whether the borrower can still be served is a credit decision, and the POS does not make it.


The documents requested follow the program. For a non-permanent resident going conventional, the[Document Concierge](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/document-concierge) asks for evidence of lawful presence the lender's policy accepts, such as an unexpired EAD or a visa with its I-94, at the same moment it asks for paystubs, not as a separate hurdle. For a permanent resident, it asks for the green card. For a citizen, it asks for nothing extra. The request is driven by what the program needs, so two borrowers with the same answer get the same request.


The status is checked against the program on every change. Residency status sits in the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) next to the loan program, so if a loan officer later moves a non-permanent resident's file from conventional to FHA, perhaps for a lower down payment, the conflict surfaces as a named exception before a case number is ordered. An FHA case number on an ineligible borrower is cheap to prevent and expensive to unwind.


## What Gets Watched After Intake


Every residency rule the agents use lives in the[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) with its source and effective date, so ML 2025-09's case-number trigger is a dated rule, not a line in a script. When a program changes, which this one did with eight weeks' notice, the change is a Rulebook edit that applies to new files from the right date and leaves earlier case numbers alone.


The same applies to what loan officers say. Our[Compliance Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/compliance-agent) scores loan-officer calls against the lender's fair lending policy, and a statement like "you need to be a citizen to buy a house" is exactly the kind of moment it cites to the timestamp. In the[deployment at a New York lender](https://www.seiright.com/case-study/sei-x-ny-mortgage-lender) , call review went from 4 calls a day to more than 1,000 a month, which means a misstatement about residency is found in the week it happens, not in a sample next quarter.


For fair lending monitoring, the useful test is the one in our post on[disparate impact and AI agents](https://www.seiright.com/blog/fair-lending-disparate-impact-ai-agents-ecoa-hmda) : compare outcomes for applicants who answered each residency category, at each stage of the funnel, and check that any difference traces to a program rule. If non-permanent residents abandon at a higher rate on a step where no program rule applies to them, that step needs looking at.


## Where This Leaves the Borrower


The borrower on the H-1B still has a path to a mortgage at most lenders, and a lender who tells them otherwise is losing a well-qualified loan and taking on fair lending risk at the same time. The rules for non-citizens now differ by program more than they have in years, which makes a single citizenship gate the wrong tool. A point of sale that asks the residency question once, uses the answer to choose programs, and explains its reasons in plain language does better by the borrower and holds up better in an exam.
